[THOUGHT] The combination of a year of burning neck/arm pain with progressive bilateral hand weakness, fasciculations, decreased upper-extremity strength and absent arm reflexes, plus a dissociated sensory loss (absent pain/temperature over chest and upper arms with preserved vibration/position sense in the hands) strongly localizes to a central cervical spinal cord lesion affecting the decussating spinothalamic fibers and anterior horn cells. Normal gait, no UMN signs in the legs, and normal Hoffmann/Babinski make generalized motor neuron disease less likely. These findings are most consistent with syringomyelia (cervical spinal cord syrinx), often due to an associated Chiari I malformation or post-traumatic/post-inflammatory syrinx. MRI of the cervical (and cervicothoracic) spine is the next definitive test but I have enough to make a single most likely diagnosis.

[THOUGHT] The clinical picture is classic for a cervical spinal cord central cord lesion producing dissociated sensory loss and lower motor neuron signs at the segmental level. Key features: bilateral loss of pain and temperature over the chest and upper arms (a "cape" distribution) with preservation of vibration/proprioception (dorsal columns intact) — indicating interruption of decussating spinothalamic fibers in the anterior commissure. Concurrent progressive weakness of the hands with fasciculations and absent upper-extremity reflexes (normal tone, no UMN signs) points to anterior horn cell involvement at the cervical segments. The chronic, progressive course localized to neck/upper limbs without leg involvement or bladder symptoms also fits a syrinx confined to the cervical cord. Alternative diagnoses (cervical radiculopathy, brachial plexopathy, ALS, transverse myelitis) do not explain the specific dissociated sensory loss pattern plus focal LMN findings as well as syringomyelia does.

[DIAGNOSIS] Syringomyelia — cervical spinal cord syrinx (most likely due to a Chiari I-related or idiopathic syrinx).

[THOUGHT] The clinical picture is suggestive of a central cervical cord process producing a "cape" distribution loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration/proprioception and progressive hand weakness — features that classically point toward syringomyelia. Findings that support syrinx: dissociated sensory loss over chest/upper arms (loss of pain/temp with preserved position/vibration), progressive hand weakness, and fasciculations (anterior horn cell involvement can occur with an expanding syrinx). Findings that conflict or are unclear: absent deep tendon reflexes in all upper extremity muscles (syrinx can give LMN findings at the level and UMN signs below — but no UMN signs are reported), normal pinprick/light touch in fingers/forearms while "pain and temperature" are reported absent over chest/upper arms (pinprick is a nociceptive test — this is internally inconsistent and needs clarification). Important differential diagnoses that remain plausible from available data include cervical myelopathy from other causes, multifocal peripheral neuropathy/plexopathy, and motor neuron disease (given fasciculations and weakness) — the sensory deficit argues against pure ALS but does not exclude mixed or concurrent pathology. No imaging or electrodiagnostic testing is available to confirm a syrinx or exclude mimics.

Red flags / critical missing data:
- No spinal MRI (cervical ± thoracic) or brain MRI to document a syrinx or Chiari malformation.
- No EMG/NCS to distinguish anterior horn cell disease from peripheral neuropathy/plexopathy or radiculopathy.
- Some inconsistency in the sensory exam (pinprick normal in fingers/forearms vs pain/temp absent over chest/upper arms) — needs clarification with repeat focused sensory mapping.
- No documentation of lower extremity reflexes, gait exam findings beyond patient report, or cranial nerve/brainstem signs.
- No timeline details for progression of fasciculations, systemic symptoms, or Valsalva-related headaches (Chiari-associated).

Given the absence of definitive imaging/electrodiagnostic evidence and the exam inconsistencies, the current information is insufficient to conclusively diagnose cervical syringomyelia.

[DECISION] INCOMPLETE

[FEEDBACK] To make a conclusive diagnosis (PASS), obtain the following critical information:
1. MRI cervical and thoracic spine with and without contrast (to visualize a syrinx and its extent). Also obtain brain MRI (posterior fossa) to evaluate for Chiari I malformation.
2. EMG and nerve conduction studies to evaluate for anterior horn cell disease (ALS) versus radiculopathy/plexopathy versus peripheral neuropathy.
3. Repeat, detailed sensory exam to resolve the inconsistency: map pinprick (pain), temperature, light touch, vibration, and proprioception by dermatomes (including fingers, forearms, shoulders, chest). Document exact dermatomal levels.
4. Full neurologic exam including lower extremity strength, tone, reflexes, gait, and cranial nerve assessment.
5. History clarifications: presence of cough/strain-induced headaches, progression timeline of fasciculations, any systemic symptoms, and any prior cervical spine imaging or trauma.
6. Consider urgent neurology/neurosurgery referral if MRI confirms syrinx or if EMG suggests motor neuron disease.

Obtain these before accepting syringomyelia as the single most likely diagnosis.

The only notable inconsistency is documented clinical fasciculations with reportedly normal needle EMG; this can occur from sampling limitations or early/segmental involvement but would warrant targeted repeat EMG if clinically needed.

- More detailed MRI report (syrinx size, extent, cord signal change, any intramedullary tumor) would be helpful to guide urgency, but the presence of a syrinx is already demonstrated.
- Correlation with targeted EMG of affected segments could clarify anterior horn involvement (sampling issue rather than refuting diagnosis).
- No current signs of lower motor neuron disease elsewhere or progressive widespread UMN signs; if such appear, re-evaluation would be required.

Overall, the MRI confirmation plus the characteristic sensory/motor pattern provide sufficient evidence for the proposed diagnosis of cervicothoracic syringomyelia.
